content: Naegleria fowleri is a free-living amoeba that thrives in warm freshwater environments, such as lakes and hot springs. It belongs to the group Percolozoa, specifically the class Heterolobosea. This organism is transmitted to humans primarily through the nasal cavity when individuals swim or dive in contaminated water. However, drinking contaminated water does not result in transmission. Naegleria fowleri is the causative agent of primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), a rare but devastating disease. The amoeba invades the human central nervous system by penetrating the cribriform plate, leading to fulminant and often fatal meningoencephalitis in the majority of cases. Taxonomy Phylum: Percolozoa Class: Heterolobosea Order: Schizopyrenida Family: Vahlkampfiidae Genus: Naegleria Species: Naegleria fowleri Binomial Name: Naegleria fowleri Biology Naegleria fowleri grows optimally at 42°C (108°F) but can tolerate temperatures as high as 45°C (113°F). Its life cycle consists of three morphological stages: 1. Trophozoite: Size: 10–30 μm. This is the infective stage, characterized by the presence of contractile vacuoles. It reproduces via binary fission. Trophozoites use pseudopodia to ingest other organisms, including red and white blood cells. 2. Cyst: Size: 7–14 μm. This is a resistant stage, protected by a dense cell wall that allows the organism to survive in harsh environmental conditions, such as cold temperatures or nutrient deprivation. Cysts can be transmitted to the human host and subsequently transform into trophozoites. Structure Naegleria fowleri is a facultatively aerobic, heterotrophic organism. In its trophozoite form, it can appear either amoeboid or flagellated. It contains several structures essential for survival and growth, including: Mitochondria Pseudopodia Flagella Contractile vacuoles Tropism Naegleria fowleri exhibits a strong tropism for the central nervous system, which is a highly oxygenated environment. The organism enters the human body through the nasal cavity and penetrates the cribriform plate. It migrates along the mesaxonal spaces of unmyelinated olfactory nerves to invade the subarachnoid spaces. Once in the subarachnoid space, it can disseminate to other regions of the central nervous system. Natural Reservoir The natural reservoirs of Naegleria fowleri are typically warm freshwater environments, such as lakes and hot springs.
